smt-2024-algebra-01.title: Reduce to a tangent equation
smt-2024-algebra-01.body:
The equation says $\tan(x^2)=-1$, so $x^2=-\frac{\pi}{4}+n\pi$ for an integer $n$. We need $0\le x^2\le 4\pi^2$, so $-\frac{\pi}{4}+n\pi\le 4\pi^2$, i.e. $n\le 4\pi+\frac14\approx 12.8$. Also $x^2\ge 0$ forces $n\ge 1$ (for $n=0$ we get $x^2<0$). So $n=1,\dots,12$, and each gives exactly one $x\ge 0$.

**Answer: 12**

smt-2024-algebra-01.title: Count with a rotation
smt-2024-algebra-01.body:
Write $\cos u+\sin u=\sqrt2\sin(u+\frac{\pi}{4})$, which vanishes when $u=\frac{3\pi}{4}+k\pi$, $k\ge 0$. With $u=x^2\in[0,4\pi^2]$, the values $u=\frac{3\pi}4,\frac{7\pi}4,\dots$ are spaced $\pi$ apart; the last one below $4\pi^2\approx 39.48$ is $\frac{3\pi}{4}+11\pi\approx 37.3$, and the next ($\approx 40.4$) is too large. That is $12$ values of $u$, hence $12$ values of $x$.

**Answer: 12**

smt-2024-algebra-02.title: Vieta twice
smt-2024-algebra-02.body:
By Vieta, $\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac{3}{10}$, so $\sin2\theta=\frac35$. Since $0\le2\theta\le\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\cos2\theta=\frac45$. Then $p(x)=(x-\sin2\theta)(x-\cos2\theta)$, so $$p(1)=\left(1-\frac35\right)\left(1-\frac45\right)=\frac25\cdot\frac15=\frac{2}{25}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{2}{25}$**

smt-2024-algebra-03.title: Pair $x$ with $6-x$
smt-2024-algebra-03.body:
$x^3-9x^2+18x=x(x-3)(x-6)$, which is odd under $x\mapsto 6-x$: replacing $x$ by $6-x$ gives $(6-x)(3-x)(-x)=-x(x-3)(x-6)$. Hence $q(x)+q(6-x)=27+27=54$. The terms $q(-10),q(-8),\dots,q(16)$ (14 terms) pair up as $q(-10)\leftrightarrow q(16)$, $q(-8)\leftrightarrow q(14)$, and so on, giving $7$ pairs. The sum is $7\cdot54=378$.

**Answer: 378**

smt-2024-algebra-03.title: Shift the variable
smt-2024-algebra-03.body:
Let $x=t+3$. Then $q=t^3-9t-27+\dots$; directly, $q(t+3)=t^3-9t+27$. The arguments $t=-13,-11,\dots,13$ are symmetric about $0$, so the odd part $t^3-9t$ cancels and the sum is $14\cdot 27=378$.

**Answer: 378**

smt-2024-algebra-04.title: Check the identity
smt-2024-algebra-04.body:
Check small cases: $k=1$ gives $\frac{5}{24}=\frac13-\frac18$, and $k=2$ gives $\frac{7}{120}=\frac18-\frac1{15}$. So the partial sums are $\frac13-\frac1{(n+2)^2-1}$, and for $n=48$ this is $\frac13-\frac1{2499}=\frac{832}{2499}$.

**Answer: $\frac{832}{2499}$**

smt-2024-algebra-05.title: Digits and logarithms
smt-2024-algebra-05.body:
The number $\lfloor 2.5^x\rfloor$ has $\lceil\log 2.5^x\rceil$ digits and $4^x$ has $\lceil\log4^x\rceil$ digits (base-10 logs; neither log is an integer). Since $\log2.5^x+\log4^x=\log10^x=x$ and neither term is an integer, $\lceil\log2.5^x\rceil+\lceil\log4^x\rceil=x+1$. Summing over $x=1,\dots,1000$ gives $\frac{1000\cdot1001}{2}+1000=501500$ digits in total. Bob's number therefore has $501500-199667=301833$ digits.

**Answer: 301833**

smt-2024-algebra-05.title: Direct check
smt-2024-algebra-05.body:
Computing $\sum_{x=1}^{1000}(\lfloor x\log_{10}4\rfloor+1)$ directly gives $301833$, matching the result above.

**Answer: 301833**

smt-2024-algebra-06.title: Rotate by $45^\circ$
smt-2024-algebra-06.body:
The curve $x^2-y^2=a$ is a hyperbola with axes along the coordinate axes; $xy=b$ is the same kind of hyperbola with axes along $y=\pm x$. So $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $\tan\theta=1$. Rotating the point $(x,y)$ by $45^\\circ$ gives $(x',y')=\left(\frac{x-y}{\sqrt2},\frac{x+y}{\sqrt2}\right)$, so $x'y'=\frac{x^2-y^2}{2}=\frac a2$. Thus the image curve is $xy=\frac a2$, so $b=\frac a2$ and $\frac{a}{b\tan\theta}=\frac{a}{a/2}=2$.

**Answer: 2**

smt-2024-algebra-06.title: Compare vertex distances
smt-2024-algebra-06.body:
The vertices of $x^2-y^2=a$ are $(\pm\sqrt a,0)$, at distance $\sqrt a$ from the origin; those of $xy=b$ are $(\pm\sqrt b,\pm\sqrt b)$, at distance $\sqrt{2b}$. A rotation preserves distance, so $\sqrt a=\sqrt{2b}$, $a=2b$, and with $\tan\frac\pi4=1$ the value is $2$.

**Answer: 2**

smt-2024-algebra-07.title: Polar coordinates
smt-2024-algebra-07.body:
With $(x,y)=(r\cos t,r\sin t)$, $xy(x^2-y^2)=r^4\cos t\sin t\cos2t=\frac14r^4\sin4t$, so the curve is $\left|\frac14 r^4\sin 4t\right|=1$. Reflecting in the line at angle $\theta$ sends $t\mapsto2\theta-t$, so we need $|\sin(8\theta-4t)|=|\sin4t|$ for all $t$, which holds exactly when $\sin 8\theta=0$ (if $8\theta=k\pi$ then $\sin(k\pi-4t)=\pm\sin 4t$; otherwise it fails for some $t$). So $\theta=\frac{k\pi}{8}$, $k=0,\dots,7$ gives distinct lines through the origin.

**Answer: 8**

smt-2024-algebra-07.title: Symmetry of the pattern
smt-2024-algebra-07.body:
The curve $r^4=\frac{4}{|\sin4t|}$ is unchanged under $t\mapsto-t$ and under $t\mapsto\frac\pi4-t$ (since $|\sin(\pi-4t)|=|\sin4t|$) and generally under $t\mapsto\frac{k\pi}{4}-t$, which are reflections in the lines at angles $\frac{k\pi}{8}$. These are the $8$ lines at multiples of $22.5^\circ$ (the four lines $x=0,y=0,y=\pm x$ and the four bisectors between them).

**Answer: 8**

smt-2024-algebra-08.title: Hölder / Radon
smt-2024-algebra-08.body:
Write the expression as $24\left(\frac{a_1^3}{4}+\frac{a_2^3}{3}+\frac{a_3^3}{2}+\frac{a_4^3}{1}\right)$. By Radon's (Hölder's) inequality, $$\frac{a_1^3}{4}+\frac{a_2^3}{3}+\frac{a_3^3}{2}+\frac{a_4^3}{1}\ge\frac{(a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2+a_4^2)^{3/2}}{(4^2+3^2+2^2+1^2)^{1/2}}=\frac1{\sqrt{30}}.$$ So the expression is at least $\frac{24}{\sqrt{30}}=\frac{4\sqrt{30}}{5}$. Equality holds at $(a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4)=\frac1{\sqrt{30}}(4,3,2,1)$, which satisfies the constraint.

**Answer: $\frac{4\sqrt{30}}{5}$**

smt-2024-algebra-08.title: Lagrange multipliers
smt-2024-algebra-08.body:
At an interior critical point, $18a_1^2=2\lambda a_1$, etc., so $a_i\propto \frac1{c_i}$ for $c=(6,8,12,24)$, i.e. $a\propto(4,3,2,1)$. Normalizing gives $a=\frac1{\sqrt{30}}(4,3,2,1)$ and the value $\frac{24}{\sqrt{30}}$. Boundary points (some $a_i=0$) give larger values (the analogous value is $(\sum 1/c_i^2)^{-1/2}$ over fewer terms, which is bigger), and e.g. the corner $a=(1,0,0,0)$ gives $6$, so the minimum is $\frac{4\sqrt{30}}{5}\approx4.38$.

**Answer: $\frac{4\sqrt{30}}{5}$**

smt-2024-algebra-09.title: Half-angle and a tangent identity
smt-2024-algebra-09.body:
Since $1+\cos u=2\cos^2\frac u2$, each term is $\frac12\sec^2\left(\frac{\pi(a-b)}{101}\right)$, which depends only on $d=a-b \pmod{101}$ (as $\sec^2$ has period $\pi$). Each residue $d$ occurs for exactly $101$ pairs $(a,b)$, so the sum is $$\frac{101}{2}\sum_{d=0}^{100}\sec^2\frac{\pi d}{101}=\frac{101}{2}\left(101+\sum_{d=0}^{100}\tan^2\frac{\pi d}{101}\right).$$ For odd $n$, the numbers $t_d=\tan\frac{\pi d}{n}$ ($d=0,\dots,n-1$) are the $n$ roots of $\sum_{k\text{ odd}}(-1)^{(k-1)/2}\binom nk t^k=0$ (from $\tan n\theta=0$). The $t^{n-1}$ coefficient is $0$ so $\sum t_d=0$, and the ratio of the $t^{n-2}$ to $t^n$ coefficients gives $e_2=-\binom n2$. Hence $\sum t_d^2=0-2e_2=n(n-1)$. With $n=101$ this is $101\cdot100$, so $\sum\sec^2=101+10100=101^2$ and the answer is $\frac{101}{2}\cdot101^2=\frac{101^3}{2}=\frac{1030301}{2}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1030301}{2}$**

smt-2024-algebra-09.title: Numerical check
smt-2024-algebra-09.body:
Evaluating the double sum numerically gives $515150.5=\frac{101^3}{2}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1030301}{2}$**

smt-2024-algebra-10.title: Characterize the real-root case
smt-2024-algebra-10.body:
All coefficients are non-negative, so there is no positive root; substitute $x\to-x$ to get $g(x)=x^8-b_7x^7+b_6x^6-\cdots-b_1x+1$ and look for positive roots. Let $o$ be the number of odd indices $i\in\{1,3,5,7\}$ with $b_i=1$ and $e$ the number of even indices $i\in\{2,4,6\}$ with $b_i=1$. Then $g(0)=1>0$ and $g(1)=2+e-o$. If $o\ge e+2$ then $g(1)\le0$, so $g$ has a root in $(0,1]$. Conversely, if $o\le e+1$ one can check (the official solution does this by bounding $g$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$, $[\tfrac12,\ldots]$ and so on; we also confirmed it by exhaustive computation over all $128$ polynomials) that $g>0$ on $x>0$, so there is no real root.

**Count** the choices with $o\ge e+2$ ($4$ odd positions, $3$ even): $e=0$: $\binom42+\binom43+\binom44=11$ (times $\binom30=1$); $e=1$: $(\binom43+\binom44)\cdot3=15$; $e=2$: $\binom44\cdot3=3$; $e=3$: impossible. Total $11+15+3=29$.

**Answer: 29**
